title: From Book to Screen
objective: After this level you can explain what a film must cut, compress or show differently when it adapts a book, and judge an adaptation on its own terms.
summary: A film must show what a book tells and fit a running time. The 1939 Wizard of Oz turned silver shoes ruby for color and made Oz a dream.

cards.headline: Why did Dorothy's silver shoes turn red?
cards.body: In L. Frank Baum's book, Dorothy's magic shoes are silver. In the 1939 film they're ruby. Nobody lost the book. The change tells you what a film has to do that a book doesn't.

cards.headline: A film has to show it
cards.body: For the 1939 film, the silver shoes became ruby, reportedly to take full advantage of color photography. Smithsonian Magazine credits screenwriter Noel Langley, probably because red would stand out against the yellow brick road. A book can call the shoes silver and move on. A film has to make you notice them, every scene.

cards.headline: A film has to fit the clock
cards.body: Level 22's rule of thumb: one page of screenplay is about one minute on screen. So a two-hour film needs about two hours' worth of script pages, whatever the length of the book behind it. A long book can't all fit, so something gets cut or compressed. The question isn't whether an adaptation cut things. It's what it chose to keep.

cards.headline: A film can change the frame
cards.body: In a departure from Baum's book, the film makes Dorothy's trip to Oz a dream, with Kansas scenes in black and white and Oz in Technicolor. That's a big change, and it's done in film's own language: color itself tells you you've crossed into another world. Judge an adaptation by what it does with its tools, not by a page count.

cards.headline: From Book to Screen: done
learned: Films must show what books tell
A page a minute forces cuts
Oz: ruby shoes, a dream, color for magic
Judge adaptations by what they do

questions.prompt: Match each with what goes with it.
questions.explanation: In Baum's book Dorothy's shoes are silver, and screenwriter Noel Langley is credited with the ruby change. The film shows its Kansas scenes in black and white and Oz in Technicolor.

questions.prompt: A studio adapts a 700-page novel into a two-hour film. Using the page-a-minute rule, what must happen?

options.label: The script will be about 700 pages
options.rationale: At a page a minute that's over eleven hours.

options.label: About two hours of pages, so much must be cut or compressed
Nothing: films always run as long as the book
The film must be split into seven parts
options.rationale: Adaptations usually cut and compress instead.

questions.explanation: At about a page a minute, two hours of film holds far fewer pages than the novel, so much is cut or compressed.

questions.prompt: Level 63's Rashomon was built from two Akutagawa short stories. What does that show about adaptation?

options.label: Adaptations must follow a single book page by page
A film can reshape its sources in its own language, as Oz did with color

questions.explanation: Like Oz turning a journey into a color-coded dream, Rashomon reshaped two stories into one film.
